Nitrogen leaks through a narrow slit into vacuum — which molecules get out?

About: Effusion of nitrogen through a slit in the wall of a box

Source

Concept
Effusion: molecules of a collisionless gas leaving one at a time through an opening into vacuum, compared with the Maxwell speed distribution of the gas left behind (Fermi Notes, §1.3, eq. 1.31).
Serves
Explaining how the speed distribution and mean kinetic energy of effusing molecules relate to those of the gas inside, at any temperature and slit size.
On screen
Top band: the box (square, slit centred in the right wall, height f × side) with its 800 N₂ molecules (m = 28.0 u) as a slowed replay in which 500 m/s moves one box width per second. Coloured dots mark the molecules that will reach the slit within the next 0.4 s, coloured by their speed vₓ towards the wall, and dashed lines stand vₓ·0.4 s from the wall for vₓ = 250, 500 and 750 m/s (in the inquiry, once question 2 is answered). Chart (with a legend): black curve = Maxwell distribution at T; grey outline = speeds inside (snapshot every 0.1 s, averaged over 5 s); blue bars = speeds of escaped molecules since the last clearing, 50 m/s bins, normalised to unit area. A kinetic-theory beam curve, ∝ v³·exp(−av²), is added once 1500 escapes have been counted. The Readouts panel below the controls shows T, f, the escape count and, from question 3, the mean kinetic energies.
Controls
T (200–500 K) re-seeds the gas and clears both histograms; slit height f (0.10–0.50, as a fraction of the wall) clears only the escaped histogram; the Clear button empties the escaped histogram.
Inquiry
Five questions to answer and then check in the sim, on the escaped histogram, its cause, the mean kinetic energy of the escapes, and the roles of temperature and slit height, followed by a summary card.
Misconception
Surfaced through each question's answer choices; each choice has its own feedback, shown only after a choice is made.
Model
The gas is collisionless (Knudsen regime), so the result holds for any slit size. A real opening wider than the mean free path lets the gas out as a jet, and the speed sorting is lost.

Pedagogy principles applied

Commit, then checkFive questions, each answered through a choice before Next opens.
Staged readoutsMean kinetic energy readouts appear only at the question that uses them; the escaped value appears once the third question is answered.
Stable axesSpeed 0–1500 m/s and density 0–3.0×10⁻³ s/m are fixed at every temperature, so every shift on the chart is physical.
Real values, labelled scalingNitrogen, m = 28.0 u, kB = 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K, SI units; the replay slowing is printed beside the box.
Operational quantitiesBars share the unit-area normalisation of the curves; energies are read in units of kBT.
Watch what stays putThe grey outline and the inside readout monitor the gas left behind throughout the leak.
Student finds the resultNo marks, lines or labels at either peak or at any crossing point.
Effusion from a Small Slit
Nitrogen box with a slit, and speed distributions

Guided Inquiry

1 · The escaped speeds

Leave the temperature at 300 K and the slit height at 0.25. Watch the blue bars build up until about 1500 molecules have escaped, comparing them with the black curve and the grey outline. How does the distribution of speeds of the escaped molecules compare with that of the gas inside?

2 · Which molecules reach the gap

Press Clear escaped histogram and watch the box and the grey outline while the blue bars build up again. Every molecule that reaches the gap leaves, and the grey outline stays on the black curve. Why do fast molecules make up a larger share of the escapes than of the gas?

3 · Energy of the escapes

Keep T = 300 K and a slit height of 0.25, clear the histogram, and let it run to about 2000 escapes. The mean kinetic energy of the molecules inside reads about 1.50 kBT. What does the mean kinetic energy of the escaped molecules settle near?

4 · Colder and hotter gas

Set T = 200 K, let about 2000 molecules escape, and read the mean kinetic energy of the escaped molecules; then set T = 500 K and do the same. How does the excess of fast molecules in the escapes change with temperature?

5 · Narrow and wide slits

Return to T = 300 K. Set the slit height to 0.10 and let about 1500 molecules escape, reading the mean kinetic energy of the escaped molecules; then widen the slit to 0.50 and do the same. What changes?

6 · What effusion does

Molecules reach an opening at a rate proportional to their speed, so the escapes are a speed-weighted sample of the gas: v³·exp(−av²) instead of v²·exp(−av²).

The beam peaks at √(3kBT/m), 1.22 times the gas peak √(2kBT/m), and carries 2kBT per molecule against 1.5kBT inside, at every temperature and slit size.

So a leaking vessel cools unless its walls resupply the energy, and at the same T lighter molecules escape faster, at a rate that goes as 1/√m.

Effusion from a Small Slit

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A gas in a box leaks through a small slit in one wall into vacuum, one molecule at a time. This sim records the speeds of the molecules that leave and sets them beside the speeds of the gas they left behind, at any temperature and any slit height.

What you'll learn

  • How the speeds of the escaped molecules compare with the speeds of the gas inside, and why.
  • How the mean kinetic energy of an escape compares with that of the gas inside.
  • What temperature and slit height each do to the escapes.
  • Where the speed distribution of a beam comes from (notes, eq. 1.31).
The set-up: a box of N₂ with a slit in the right-hand wall, and vacuum beyond.

What's on screen

  • The box (top band): 800 N₂ molecules (m = 28.0 u) that never collide, replayed slowly: 500 m/s crosses one box width a second. Escapes fly on as blue dots that fade.
  • Black curve: the Maxwell speed distribution of the gas at T. Grey outline: the speeds actually inside the box, averaged over the last 5 s.
  • Blue bars: speeds of the molecules that have escaped since the last clearing, in 50 m/s bins. The blue curve is the theory curve for effusion.
  • Readouts: T, f, the escape count Nesc and the mean kinetic energies.
See itEmpty the blue histogram and let the escapes build up, with your current T and f. Watch for: blue dots leaving through the slit, while the escape counter and the blue bars on the chart grow.

Fixed: nitrogen, m = 28.0 u, with 800 molecules. The walls re-emit molecules at T, and each molecule that escapes is replaced by one sent in at T from a random point of the right wall beside the slit. That makes up for the molecules the open slit no longer sends back, so the gas inside stays at T and close to uniform, and the escape rate and the speeds of the escapees are those the effusion formula gives. The density is not exactly even: at the widest slit it runs about 30% low beside the slit and about 30% high in the right-hand corners, while the left half of the box stays within about 3% of the mean.

03

Escapes are not a fair sample of the gas

A slit that is small compared with the mean free path lets molecules go one at a time, without disturbing the gas inside. The molecules that leave are the ones that would have struck that piece of wall. They are not a fair sample of the gas: the beam is richer in fast molecules. (The sim's molecules never collide, so no slit makes a jet, and each escaped molecule is replaced from the wall beside the slit, so even at the widest slit the gas inside stays at T and close to uniform.)

The gas curve goes as v² e−mv²/2kBT. The beam carries one extra factor of v (notes, 1.31), so it peaks higher. At 300 K the gas peaks at √(2kBT/m) = 422 m/s and the beam at √(3kBT/m) = 517 m/s. About 10% of the gas is faster than 750 m/s, but about 18% of the beam is.

Notes (1.31). The gas inside has v² where the beam has v³.
Both curves for N₂ at 300 K, each with unit area. The dotted line marks 750 m/s: the area of the beam curve beyond it is the larger.
See itEmpty the histogram and let the escapes build up, with your current T and f. Watch for: the blue bars piling up around the blue curve, to the right of the black curve’s peak.
04

Fast molecules reach the slit from further away

Every molecule that arrives at the slit leaves, fast or slow: the slit sorts nothing. The sorting happens before the slit, in how many molecules of each speed arrive.

In a short time Δt a molecule with velocity component vx towards the wall reaches it only if it starts within vxΔt of it. A fast molecule is collected from a thick slab, a slow one from a thin slab, so more fast molecules are within reach. Averaged over directions, that weight is proportional to the speed v. Arrivals are therefore weighted by speed, which is the extra factor of v.

Molecules at the far edge of each slab just reach the slit in Δt. The slab behind the fast molecule is almost three times as thick.

The sim draws this. Its dashed lines, labelled 250, 500 and 750, stand 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 box widths from the slit wall: the depth vxΔt for those values of vx (m/s), with Δt = 0.4 s of replay. Dots mark the molecules that will reach the slit within Δt, coloured by vx.

See itLet the replay run with your current T and f. Watch for: red and purple dots out beyond the 500 line, while yellow dots appear only inside the 250 line.
05

The escapes carry 2kBT on average

Inside the box the mean kinetic energy is 3/2 kBT per molecule. Because fast molecules are over-represented among the escapes, each escape carries more. Averaging ½mv² over the beam distribution v³ e−av² gives exactly 2kBT, whatever the temperature.

The gas inside averages to 3/2 kBT, with v² in place of v³.

In the sim, Readouts shows about 1.50 kBT for the box and about 2.00 kBT for the escaped molecules. The escaped value is a running mean over the molecules counted so far, so it wanders by a few hundredths until a thousand or more have escaped.

A real vessel that leaks this way therefore cools, unless its walls supply the difference. In the sim the walls are held at T and replace every escaped molecule, so the gas inside stays at 1.50 kBT.

See itEmpty the histogram with your T, and widen the slit to f = 0.50 so the count rises faster. Watch for: Escaped molecules settling near 2.00 kBT while Inside the box stays near 1.50.
06

Heating moves both peaks together

Temperature enters only through a = m/2kBT, which sets the speed scale. Both peaks go as √T, so their ratio stays √(3/2) = 1.22 at every temperature. From 200 K to 500 K both peaks rise by √(500/200) = 1.58: the gas from 345 to 545 m/s, the beam from 422 to 667 m/s.

Peak speeds of the gas and of the beam against T. The beam stays 1.22 times above the gas.

The gap in m/s widens, from 77 m/s at 200 K to 122 m/s at 500 K, but the excess of fast molecules is a ratio, not a fixed speed. The mean energies do not move in units of kBT: about 1.50 inside and about 2.00 escaped, at both ends. The chart's speed axis is fixed at 0 to 1500 m/s, so every shift you see is physical.

See itCool the gas to 200 K, keeping your slit height. Watch for: both curves moving left, the black one to 345 m/s and the blue one to 422 m/s.
See itHeat the gas to 500 K, keeping your slit height. Watch for: both curves moving right, the black one to 545 m/s and the blue one to 667 m/s.
07

The slit sets the rate, not the speeds

The escape rate is proportional to the area of the hole (notes, 1.30): in the sim, to the slit height f. At 300 K the sim lets out about 19 molecules a second at f = 0.10 and about 95 a second at f = 0.50 at 1× speed: five times as many.

Notes (1.30). n is the number density and A the area of the hole.

The speeds do not change. A wider slit collects more molecules, each still weighted by its speed, so the bars keep their shape and the mean stays near 2.00 kBT.

See itSet T = 300 K and the narrow slit, f = 0.10. Watch for: the count rising by about 19 each second.
See itSet T = 300 K and the wide slit, f = 0.50. Watch for: the count rising by about 95 each second, with the bars in the same shape.
08

Where it matters

  • Isotope separation. Since v̄ = √(8kBT/πm), the lighter isotope of a gas effuses a little faster, in the ratio √(m2/m1). One stage gains very little, so uranium hexafluoride was passed through cascades of thousands of stages (notes, section 1.3).
  • Molecular beams. An oven with a small opening is a standard source of an atomic or molecular beam. Its speeds follow the v³ shape, not the Maxwell shape of the gas in the oven.
  • A leaking vessel. Each escape carries 2kBT against 3/2 kBT for the gas, so an insulated vessel cools as it leaks.
Go deeper: when the opening is not small

Effusion needs a hole small compared with the mean free path. A wider hole lets the gas out as a jet, with collisions in the opening, and the speed sorting is lost. The sim's gas has no collisions, so its slit never makes a jet, and f changes only the rate.

09

Summary

In one line. Effusion is escape through a hole small compared with the mean free path, and this sim sets what leaves beside the gas left behind.

Key points

  • The escapes go as v³ e−av², the gas as v² e−av²: arrivals at the slit are weighted by speed.
  • At 300 K the peaks are 517 and 422 m/s; both go as √T and their ratio stays 1.22.
  • An escape carries 2kBT on average, against 3/2 kBT inside, at every T and f.
  • The slit height sets the rate, in proportion to f, and nothing else.

Common mix-ups

  • “The escapes have the same speeds as the gas.” They peak at 517 m/s against 422 m/s at 300 K.
  • “The escapes carry the average energy of the gas.” They carry 2.00 kBT, against 1.50 kBT inside.
  • “A wider slit lets out faster molecules.” It lets out more of them, five times as many at f = 0.50 as at 0.10, with the same speeds.

Things to try on your own

  • At T = 400 K, let about 1500 molecules escape. Compare the tallest blue bars with √(3kBT/m) = 597 m/s.
  • Time 100 escapes at f = 0.10, then at f = 0.50. Compare the two times.
  • At f = 0.50, read both energy readouts after 2000 escapes and subtract them. Compare with 2 − 3/2.
